title: SDK Bridgehead: 10x Quickstart Experiments
content:
Purpose:
Rapid, observable experiments to cut new-developer time-to-first-success (TTFS) in the SDK flow by 10x for common use-cases (text generation, chat, embeddings). This doc is a compact playbook: three runnable 10-minute labs, measurement hooks, acceptance criteria, and next-step proposals.

Audience:
- Developer advocates running onboarding sessions
- Developer experience engineers shipping starter kits
- Solutions engineers preparing customer POCs

Why this deck exists (short):
We regularly hear: "it should just work in 5 minutes". Current TTFS is ~8–12 minutes for a basic hello world (with installing deps, API key, sample app). The Bridgehead experiments focus on removing friction in three orthogonal areas: environment bootstrap, local fidelity (stubbed runtime), and prompt + eval scaffolding.

Success metrics (observable):
- Primary: median TTFS per new user <= 60s for the "Hello Generate" path in lab environment.
- Secondary: >= 90% of participants complete the quick-validations checklist in a single session without intervention.
- Measurement: instrument runs via a short opt-in telemetry ping (start, deps-installed, hello-req-sent, hello-req-ok).

Quick summary of the three experiments
1) Zero-config starter (packaged environment)
   - Goal: Ship a single archive that unpacks and runs a local static sample app that calls hosted API with no install step beyond unzipping.
   - Components: prebuilt binary (tiny node app), embedded sample prompt, cached lightweight cert bundle for TLS to local-proxy.
   - Acceptance: Unpack -> double-click/run -> "Hello from Redwood" response in < 60s on mac/linux.

2) Local-stub fidelity (fast offline simulation)
   - Goal: Provide a hermetic stub server that returns realistic streaming-like responses and KV cache behavior so developers can iterate offline.
   - Components: simple stub (go binary), minimal corpus of sample tokens to exercise streaming and function-calls, a client shim pre-wired to detect stub and switch telemetry to dev mode.
   - Acceptance: Developer sees a progressive streamed response and can toggle to hosted API with one env var.

3) Prompt-eval micro-harness (instant validation)
   - Goal: Surface a tiny test harness that verifies output quality against 3 golden prompts and shows token cost estimates.
   - Components: three canonical prompts (summarize, extract, rerank), evaluation runner (node/python script), a small UI that displays pass/fail + example diff.
   - Acceptance: Run harness -> green/red badges + suggested next steps in < 2 minutes.

10-minute lab runbooks (practical steps)
Lab A: Zero-config starter (target: 5–10 minutes)
 - 0:00–0:30: unzip bridgehead-starter.tgz, open README.txt
 - 0:30–1:30: double-click run-bridgehead (or ./run-bridgehead.sh)
 - 1:30–2:30: confirm sample page opened at http://localhost:5622 (shows sample prompt and button)
 - 2:30–3:30: click "Run Hello Generate" -> observe streamed token-by-token output in sample console
 - 3:30–6:00: poke settings -> switch model variant -> rerun -> note latency/prompt differences
 - 6:00–10:00: optional: open troubleshooting panel showing packaged logs and a single-click "collect and share" that uploads to a private gist for debugging (opt-in)

Lab B: Local-stub fidelity (target: 8–12 minutes)
 - 0:00–1:00: git clone stub-harness and run ./stub --port=1717 or double-click stub-runner
 - 1:00–3:00: run client sample that hits the stub; observe streaming simulated output and message chunk timings
 - 3:00–5:00: flip env to REDWOOD_LOCAL_STUB=true and re-run sample app -> confirm smooth fallback
 - 5:00–8:00: run a simulated eviction of KV cache in the stub and observe client recovery (telemetry event KV_CACHE_RESET)
 - 8:00–12:00: capture metrics and file a smoke test via provided make smoke (generates a small report)

Lab C: Prompt-eval micro-harness (target: 4–6 minutes)
 - 0:00–0:30: download eval bundle or run npx redwood-eval quickstart
 - 0:30–1:30: run eval --prompts golden-set --report=console
 - 1:30–3:00: read the pass/fail badges and expand diff for the failing item
 - 3:00–6:00: accept suggested remediation (e.g., change prompt template, increase temperature) and re-run

Developer-first UX heuristics used here
 - Opt-out telemetry: minimal events for TTFS measurement, with explicit consent and ephemeral IDs.
 - One-click collect: packaged diagnostic that doesn't require copying logs.
 - Toggle parity: single env var to swap between stub/local and hosted API with no code change.
 - Mini-guides: in-app micro-help cards that show the next 3 steps rather than a big page.

Instrumentation & telemetry schema (brief)
Events (opt-in): ["lab_start","deps_installed","http_request_sent","http_response_ok","eval_run","kb_share_click"]
Fields collected (minimal): ["client_os","lab_id","duration_ms","success_bool","model_variant"]
Retention: 7 days for lab debugging; aggregated metrics kept for product improvement.

Smoke tests & CI gating
- Add a nightly job that runs the zero-config starter in headless mode on linux and mac runners.
- If TTFS (headless) > 120s for median of 5 runs, auto-open ENG-1145 (example ticket).

Known risks and mitigations
- Packaging size: shipping prebuilt binaries increases repo size. Mitigation: host artifacts on CDN and fetch the first time with a progress bar.
- Local TLS issues: older macOS versions may block. Mitigation: fallback to non-TLS local mode and call that out prominently.
- Telemetry opt-in friction: keep it off by default and highlight the benefit (faster issue resolution).

Open questions / decisions to make
 - Do we want a single monolithic artifact per OS or a small bootstrapper that downloads the tiny pieces? (trade-off: offline vs download latency)
 - How aggressive should auto-updates be for the stub? (silent vs explicit)
 - Scope for additional golden prompts per vertical (customer-supplied) or keep a single core set?

Next steps (short roadmap)
1) Week 1: build artifacts for mac/linux, create sample starter PR (owner: @maya).
2) Week 2: integrate telemetry opt-in dialog and add nightly CI smoke.
3) Week 3: run 3 customer sessions with SEs and capture TTFS.
4) Week 4: iterate on packaging based on feedback and aim for a pilot-ready tag.

Quick troubleshooting reference (common fixes)
 - If app doesn't start: check port collisions (run lsof -i :5622) and kill offending process.
 - If streaming looks choppy: confirm REDWOOD_LOCAL_STUB=true vs hosted; stub sim has an artificial chunk delay configurable with STUB_CHUNK_MS.
 - If eval fails with rate-limit: switch to stub mode for the quick run or use the small eval corpus.

Scratchpad notes from the last pairing session:
- Noah: suggested adding an in-app "copy prompt" cheat for non-dev PMs.
- Maya: will prototype the one-click collect + private gist flow.
- Sofia: recommended a smaller default model variant for first-run to reduce cost and latency.

If you run these labs, please paste short TTFS results and OS in the #devexp-quickstart Slack thread and tag @Riley.

Appendix: sample CLI commands (copy-paste)
 - Unpack & run (mac/linux): tar -xzf bridgehead-starter.tgz && ./run-bridgehead.sh
 - Run stub locally: ./stub --port=1717 &
 - Eval quick run: npx redwood-eval --quickstart

End of doc.
